title: Your role

list: You own the conversation with the owner, from first touch to signed pilot.
Success: owners see their own leak, say yes to the Level 1 pilot, and keep it past day 30.
You do not build, you do not promise features, you do not discount.
If it is not live, you do not sell it as live.

notes:
Say: "This job is simple to describe and hard to do well. You find owners who are already paying for leads and losing them to slow answers. You show them the leak with their own numbers. You get a yes on the pilot. That is it. The build is ours. The promises are limited to what is on the status slides."
Say: "Three things you never do. You never promise a feature that is not live. You never offer a discount or a free trial. You never quote a price other than the Level 1 pilot until I confirm the rest."
Say: pay terms for the role are settled between you and me separately. Do not improvise them on this slide.
Ask the rep: "In your own words, what is the one thing you would never say to an owner on a first call?" Listen for a guarantee, a free trial, or a feature that is not live.

title: What we sell in one sentence

list: Every lead answered in minutes, at any hour.
Carried to a booking or a payment.
A person takes over the moment it matters.
Proof of how fast, in the owner's own numbers.

notes:
Say: "This is the sentence. Say it until it is boring. The owner does not want AI. The owner wants the lead answered before the competitor picks up, and a booked job on the calendar."
Say: we sell the outcome: a lead that gets an answer, then a booking. We do not lead with the tool or the setup.
Say: the target first reply is five minutes, set per business at onboarding. It is a target we measure and report, not a guarantee.
Ask the rep: "Say the sentence back to me without the word AI." If he can, move on.

title: The problem

list: Owners pay for leads: ads, directories, web forms.
Then the lead waits. The owner is on a job, on the mat, or asleep.
Whoever answers first usually gets the job.
How long does YOUR lead wait? We time it.

notes:
Say: "The owner already did the hard, expensive part. They paid to get the lead. The money is lost in the gap between the lead arriving and a human answering."
Say: "Speed decides who wins the job" is the argument. Do not add a statistic to it. Vendor blogs quote big multipliers. They are not ours to repeat, and some measure a different thing than sales. The only number we use is the prospect's own audit number, from the free proof on slide 12.
Say: the strongest line in the whole deck is the owner's own response time, measured by us, shown to them.
Ask the rep: "If an owner says speed does not matter in their trade, what do you ask next?" Good answer: "When you shop for a plumber at 9 pm, who do you call back?" or "Show me your last ten leads and when each got a reply."

title: How it works

list: 1. A lead arrives from any channel.
2. It becomes one lead record. Duplicates are merged. Consent is checked.
3. First reply goes out inside the response window.
4. Follow-up continues until booked, replied, or opted out.
5. A person takes over when it matters. Booking or payment closes it. A report shows the speed.

notes:
Status: the console, the database with a separate space per client, approvals, inbox, handoffs, meetings and the email path are built. The lead record pipeline (S2L-1 and S2L-1b) is built and under audit, not live. Channel adapters are designed. See slide 5.
Say, plainly, for a skeptical owner:
- "A lead can arrive as a form, an ad form, an email, a text, a DM, a call. We turn every one into the same kind of record, so the system treats them the same way. The glossary calls this a lead event."
- "Before we send anything, we check if we already have this person (so nobody gets two texts) and whether we have a valid reason to contact them (the consent basis). No reason, no message."
- "The first reply goes out inside the response window. The default is five minutes. We set it per business."
- "Then a follow-up ladder runs: for example text, then email, then a call attempt. It stops when the person books, replies in a way that needs a human, opts out, or hits a daily cap. Nothing loops forever."
- "Anytime the lead asks for a human, or the topic is an emergency, a big job, a complaint, or a price only a person may quote, the owner or staff gets an alert with the whole thread and a suggested next move."
- "Last, the lead ends as booked, paid, handed to a person, opted out, or closed. Results shows how fast the first reply was, per channel."
Ask the rep: "Walk me through what happens to a web form lead at 11:40 pm." Expected: record created, duplicate and consent check, text and email within seconds, owner alerted, callback attempt if no reply, booking if the lead says yes. Status: each step depends on the adapters on slide 5.

title: Three response modes

list: Text: first reply in minutes, missed-call text-back, follow-up until they book. (designed, needs approval)
Social conversion: a comment opens a DM, the DM books the job. (designed, needs approval)
Voice receptionist: answers or calls back, books, texts the owner a summary. (designed, needs approval)
Email and web forms feed all three. (email built, forms designed)

notes:
Say: "Three ways to answer, one brain behind them. Text is the workhorse. Social conversion is for owners who live on Instagram, like martial arts schools: someone comments a keyword, gets a public 'sent you a DM' and a private message that qualifies and books. Voice is the receptionist that answers when nobody can, books, and texts the owner a summary."
Say: automated social messages say they are automated. Voice announces recording where the law requires it. That is built into the design, not an afterthought.
Say: pick the lead mode by niche. Owners buying ads: form response time. Owners who miss calls on job sites: missed-call text-back. Schools and creators: comment to DM.
Say: until a channel clears its outside approval, a pilot uses what is ready and the owner is told so in writing.
Ask the rep: "Which mode would you open with for a generator dealer? A martial arts school?" Expected: dealer, missed calls and form response; school, comment to DM and form response.

title: Follow-through

list: A person can step in at any point, on any channel.
Booking with real open slots, confirmation, reminders, and no-show handling.
Payment options the owner turns on: pay link, deposit, quote then invoice, or pay later (the default).
The owner's own payment account. The money never passes through us.

notes:
Status: Handoffs and Meetings pages are built. Alerts, warm transfer, resume-to-agent, calendar slots, reminders and no-show handling are designed. Payments are designed and need approval (a payment provider design and the client's own account; no code yet).
Say: "The agent does not stop at 'interested'. It carries the lead to a finished outcome. When a person has the thread, the agent goes silent on it. A button gives it back."
Say: "On payments, the default is pay later or on site. Pay-now links, deposits and quote-then-invoice are opt-in, per client. Card details never touch us. Anything over a limit the client sets, or anything not on their list, needs a person to approve it. Refunds and disputes are human only."
Say: do not promise payments in a pilot. It is a later module.
Ask the rep: "An owner says 'I only want it to book, not take money.' Is that a problem?" Expected: no, that is the default.

title: Safety and consent

list: Every channel starts off. The owner approves it first.
Week one is approval mode: every draft waits for a yes.
A send lock stays on until we release it.
Every contact needs a consent basis. No basis, no message.
Opt-outs and bounces block that person everywhere. Daily caps. Quiet hours.

notes:
Say: "This is why it is not spam. It is targeted and qualified, it asks permission first, and it has brakes."
- "Approval mode: for the first week the owner or we approve what goes out. They see every message before the lead does."
- "Send lock: nothing sends until we flip it on, per client and per channel."
- "Suppression: if someone opts out, bounces, or complains, that contact is blocked on every channel."
- "Caps: a daily limit per client, and quiet hours. No blasting."
- "Consent basis on every lead record. A form with consent language, a call they made to the business, a list the owner has a right to contact. We hand them the consent line to add to their forms."
Rep one-liner for nervous owners: "It only replies to people who already reached out to you, it stops the moment they say stop, and for the first week you approve every message before it goes."
Do not say: that it is legally guaranteed compliant. Say it is built to follow consent and opt-out rules and that the owner approves everything first.
Ask the rep: "An owner asks 'will this get me sued?' What do you say, and what do you not say?" Good answer uses the one-liner and avoids any legal promise.

title: Who we sell to

list: Generator dealers
Martial arts schools
Remodelers (aging in place, one-day bath)
The filter inside every niche: the owner already runs ads, outreach, or web forms, and has no speed to lead in place.
Skip: crowded answering niches, franchises, anyone who wants a free trial.

notes:
Say: "These are the three niches the Blueprint picked. In each one the miss costs far more than the pilot, the owner is the bottleneck, and they can say yes in one conversation."
Say: the sharpened filter, in plain words: the best target is an owner already paying for lead flow, through ads, directories, outreach or web forms, whose first reply is slow or manual. The leads already arrive. The reply is the weak part. The audit proves it by timing their own form or ad lead.
Niche notes:
- Generator dealers. Phone first. Calls come at bad hours, especially around outages. Lead with missed calls and form response. Low local count, so winners go beyond the home metro early.
- Martial arts schools. Instagram is their storefront. Lead with trial-class bookings, comment to DM and form response. Lower monthly prices in this niche, so watch the fit on very small schools.
- Remodelers. Pay for leads and write estimates that go quiet. Lead with lead reply speed and estimate follow-up. Outcome pricing is the draft fit here (slide 13).
Skip list (Blueprint and Full-Context disqualifiers): franchise headquarters controls phones or vendors, a team already covers nights, owner unreachable, typical job very small, demands a custom build, wants licensed advice in the script, wants a free trial. Crowded markets such as HVAC and plumbing answering, med spas and hearing clinics are on the avoid list.
Say: market sizes and job values in the Blueprint are planning assumptions. Do not quote them to a prospect. Ask the owner for their own average job value.
Ask the rep: "A martial arts school with no ads, no forms, and four students. Do we call?" Expected: no, the filter fails.

title: Finding and qualifying

list: Signals: running ads, a lead form on the site, a "get a quote" button, reviews that mention slow replies, a voicemail greeting.
Where: ad libraries, the business's site and socials, Google Maps and reviews, local owner groups.
Five questions to qualify (below).

head: Question
A good answer sounds like
rows: Where do your leads come from today?
Ads, directories, forms, calls. More than one source.
Who answers them, and when?
The owner, on the job or after hours. No one at night.
What is a typical job worth to you?
A number high enough that one lost lead hurts.
How many leads slip each month, roughly?
An honest guess, or "I do not know". Both work.
If we showed you the real number, who decides?
The person on the call.

notes:
Say: "You are looking for proof of spend and proof of slowness. If you see both before you call, the call is easy."
Where to look, in practice (all free, public, and allowed):
- Ad libraries for the business name: are they running ads?
- Their website: a form, a phone number, a chat widget, a booking link. Note what happens when you do not hit it.
- Google reviews and Maps: look for lines like "could never get through" or "no one called back".
- Instagram and Facebook pages: a trial offer, a quote post, and whether comments sit unanswered.
- Local owner groups and associations, to find owners, not to pitch in public threads.
Do not do: submit a prospect's form or call their line yourself outside the audit process on slide 12. The audit is run by us, once, with a plan.
Say: the qualifying questions are a conversation, not a form. Question 4 is the key: it opens the leak without us claiming a number.
Say: if question 5 is "my partner decides", ask for the partner on the results call.
Ask the rep: "Name three signals you can check in ten minutes before calling a dealer." Check that he names ads, a form, and a slow or unanswered channel.

title: The free proof

list: Level 0, free: a missed-call audit and a response-time test.
We call their line and time their own web form.
We hand back what a caller hears and how long a lead waits.
It ends in a 20-minute results call.

notes:
Status: a manual process with no build needed. It is the first thing we do for every prospect, and the only free thing we give.
How to run it, in order:
1. Pick a time when the owner is likely busy or the office is closed. Write down the time before you act.
2. Call the main line once. Note how many rings, voicemail or a live answer, what the greeting says, whether a text or call comes back, and how long it took.
3. Submit the business's own web form once, with a clearly labelled test contact that is ours. Record the exact submit time and the time of the first reply of any kind. An auto-reply counts as an auto-reply. A real answer from a person counts separately.
4. Never repeat the call or the form. Never call a private mobile. Never use another person's details.
5. Optional: a dormant-list sample analysis, only if the owner offers a list. Counts only, no outreach.
What to hand over: a one-page summary and a short screen recording, with times. Their numbers, not ours.
How it becomes the results call: book 20 minutes. Show the times. Ask what a lost job is worth to them. Do the arithmetic with their number: average job value times leads missed in a month, labelled as an estimate. Then offer the Level 1 pilot.
Say: "The proof is free so the price conversation starts from your numbers, not mine."
Do not say that the audit predicts bookings. It shows the gap, nothing more.
Ask the rep: "What do you do if their form answers instantly?" Good answer: say so honestly, then look at calls, after hours and follow-up depth. If every channel is fast, the filter fails and we move on.

title: The sales path
body: Gate: 20 conversations with fewer than 2 paid pilots means we rotate the niche.
notes:
Each step in one line:
1. First touch: short, about their business, one question. Never a pitch in the first message.
2. Discovery: slide 16 questions. Find the leak and the decision maker.
3. Free proof: slide 12. Our work, their numbers.
4. Results call: 20 minutes. Show the times. Do the math with their job value.
5. Proposal: the Level 1 pilot, $499 flat, 30 days.
6. Sign: pilot agreement, consent language agreed, payment first.
7. Onboard: slide 19.
Targets (planning assumptions from the Blueprint, never measured, so targets to test and not promises): about 20 conversations per 100 outreach attempts. One niche gets one cycle of 100 attempts. The gate: after 20 real conversations, fewer than 2 paid pilots means the niche rotates. We track attempts, conversations, audits done, results calls held and pilots signed.
Say: "We rotate on facts. If it is not working in a niche, we change niche. We do not discount to force it."
Open item for Christian: the pilot start-date policy until go-live (manual-assist pilot, or a waitlist with a fixed start date) is undecided. Give owners no start date until it is.
Ask the rep: "Where do most deals die, and what do you do about it?" Use the answer to tune the order.

title: Discovery questions

head: Ask
What the answer tells you
rows: Where do your leads come from?
Whether they already pay for lead flow. Ads, forms and directories are the fit.
What happens when a lead comes in at night or while you are on a job?
Where the gap is and who covers it.
How fast does the first reply go out, honestly?
Their own view of speed. Often slower than they think.
Who replies today: owner, staff, a tool?
Who decides and who feels the pain.
What is an average job worth?
The number we use on the results call.
How many leads do you think slip each month?
Their sense of the leak. "No idea" is fine.
What have you tried to fix it?
Past tools, past failures, objections coming.
Who else decides?
Whether the results call needs a second person.
If we showed you the real numbers, what would you do?
Whether they act on proof.

notes:
Say: "Ask, then be quiet. Write down their exact words. You will use those words on the results call."
Opening script: "I help local service businesses answer every lead fast, at any hour. Before I tell you anything, I would like to understand how it works for you today. Can I ask a few questions?"
Red flags: no ads, no forms and few leads; a team already covers nights; the owner cannot be reached; the typical job is very small; wants a custom build or licensed advice in the script; wants a free trial. Two or more: thank them and move on.
Green flags: pays for leads; answers his own phone; says "I miss calls on jobs"; reviews mention slow replies.
Do not quote the system's speed in numbers until we have measured theirs.
Ask the rep: "An owner says we answer everything within a few minutes. What does that tell you, and what is your next question?" Expected: ask how they know, and offer the response-time test.

title: Objections and answers
body: Six objections, one answer each. Full scripts are in the notes.
notes:
Method: agree with the concern, answer in two sentences, bring it back to their own numbers, ask one question. Never argue.

1. "$499 is a lot."
"Fair question. The pilot is priced against one job, not against software. What is a typical job worth to you? [listen] So if this saves even one lead a month you would not otherwise have gotten, the pilot has paid for itself. We measure it in booked jobs and show you at day 14."
2. "We already have a CRM or software that does this."
"Good, keep it. We do not replace it. We sit in front of it and handle the first reply, the follow-up and the booking. A CRM stores leads. It does not answer them at 9 pm. Can I time your form so we both see what actually happens?"
3. "AI feels cheap. My customers want a person."
"They do, and they get one. The first reply is fast so nobody is left waiting, and a person takes over the moment the lead asks, the job is big, or it is a complaint. For the first week you approve every message before it goes. Would you rather a lead wait six hours for a person, or hear back in minutes and then reach a person?"
4. "We answer fast enough."
"Great, then the free check will show it. We time your own form and your own line and give you the numbers. If you are fast, you will know. If there is a gap at night or on a job, you will see that too. Who covers after hours today?"
5. "I worry about spam."
"Same concern we have. It only replies to people who already reached out to you. Every message carries a stop option, anyone who says stop is blocked everywhere, there are daily limits and quiet hours, and for the first week you approve each message. No blasting, no bought lists."
6. "What if it says something wrong?"
"It only works from a playbook we build with you: your services, your hours, what it may say and what it may not. Prices and special cases go to a person. For the first week nothing goes out without your approval, and you can take over any conversation at any time. We review the week together."

Also useful:
- "Send me info." Reply: "Info does not book jobs. Let me run the free check first. It takes me one call and one form, and you will see your own numbers."
- "I am too small." Reply: "Small is who this fits. You are the bottleneck, and one booked job changes your month."
Never use in an answer: a statistic, a competitor's price, a guarantee, a discount.
Ask the rep: "Give me objection 4 in your own words and I will play the owner." Role-play two rounds.

title: Never say

list: No guarantees of bookings, revenue or results.
No statistics we cannot source. Use the owner's own audit number.
No channel that is not live. Check slide 5 and the status board with Christian.
No discounts. No free trials. Ever.
No competitor prices.
No legal or compliance promises.

notes:
Say: "These six rules protect you and us. If a prospect pushes, the answer is always the same: we measure it, we show you at day 14, and you decide from your own numbers."
Swaps:
- "We guarantee more bookings" becomes "We measure booked jobs and show you at day 14."
- "Studies show fast replies win far more leads" becomes "We will time your own leads." Do not repeat a vendor multiplier, even if the owner has seen one.
- "We do Instagram and texting" becomes "Those channels need approval from the platform or carrier. They are coming, and they are added when cleared. Here is what is ready now."
- "I can do it for less" becomes "The pilot is $499, flat. It is the same for everyone."
- "Try it free for a week" becomes "The free proof is the free part. The pilot is the proof you pay for."
- "We are cheaper than X" becomes "We price against one job, not against software."
- "It is fully compliant" becomes "It is built around consent and opt-out, and you approve every message in week one."
- "We recovered $X for you" becomes "Estimated value, using your own job average."
Ask the rep: "Which of these is hardest for you to hold?" Work on that one.

Report content: leads in, median and slowest first reply per channel, replies, bookings, estimated value (labelled as an estimate).
Ask the rep: "An owner wants to go live tomorrow. What must be true first?" Expected: signed agreement, consent line on forms, access granted, test passed, and Christian has released the send lock.

Suggested day: 15 minutes on yesterday's numbers; outreach blocks; calls and discovery; audits using the slide 12 plan; results calls; end of day update of the log and anything to flag.
Numbers to log every day: attempts, conversations, audits run, results calls held, pilots proposed, pilots signed, the exact words of each objection, and the niche of each.
Who to call for what:
- Price, scope, anything not on these slides: Christian.

title: Glossary

head: Term
Plain meaning
rows: Lead event
One record of "someone reached out", whatever channel it came from.
First touch
The first reply to a new lead. We time it.
Response window
How fast the first reply should go out. Default 5 minutes, set per business.
Consent basis
The reason we may contact this person: they filled in a form, they called, or the owner has a right to contact them. No basis, no message.
Suppression
A do-not-contact list. Opt-outs, bounces and complaints are blocked on every channel.
Handoff
A person takes over the conversation and the agent goes quiet.
Approval mode
Every draft message waits for a yes before it goes out. Week one.
A2P (10DLC)
The carrier registration US business texting needs. It takes weeks and is outside our control.
Plugin / adapter
One channel's connection to the core, for example web form or email.
Idempotent
Safe to repeat: the same event arriving twice makes one lead, not two.

notes:
Say: "If an owner uses one of these words, you can answer in one line. If they do not, do not use them."
Two extra words may come up. Playbook: the client's rules for the agent, covering services, tone and what must go to a person. Send lock: the switch that keeps all sending off until Christian releases it.
Ask the rep: "Explain consent basis and suppression to me as if I were a plumber." One sentence each.

How to run it in front of a prospect:
1. Open it on your own screen first, the same day. Never share a screen into something you have not tested that day.
2. Pick the sample business closest to the prospect's trade.
3. Start a session, play the lead, and let the prospect watch the reply.
4. Point at three things: how quickly it replies, how it asks the qualifying questions, and where it hands off to a person.
5. Then go straight back to their own numbers from the audit.
